claim: Five neurosurgical patients undergoing treatment for epilepsy had invasive electrocorticography (ECoG) electrodes implanted to measure neural activity.
source: To study the nonlinear receptive fields of auditory cortical responses, we used invasive electrocorticography (ECoG) to directly measure neural activity from five neurosurgical patients undergoing treatment for epilepsy.
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section describing the patient cohort and recording technique.

claim: One patient had high-density subdural grid electrodes implanted on the left hemisphere with coverage primarily over the superior temporal gyrus (STG).
source: One patient had high-density subdural grid electrodes implanted on the left hemisphere, with coverage primarily over the superior temporal gyrus (STG).
evidence: Directly stated description of electrode placement in one patient.

claim: All five patients had depth electrodes (stereotactic EEG) with coverage of Heschl's gyrus (HG) and STG.
source: All five patients had depth electrodes (stereotactic EEG) with coverage of Heschl's gyrus (HG) and STG (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: HG includes the primary auditory cortex.
source: HG includes the primary auditory cortex, while the STG is considered mostly a nonprimary auditory cortical area (Clarke and Architecture, 2012).
evidence: Stated with citation to support the anatomical classification.

claim: The STG is considered mostly a nonprimary auditory cortical area.
source: HG includes the primary auditory cortex, while the STG is considered mostly a nonprimary auditory cortical area (Clarke and Architecture, 2012).
evidence: Stated with citation to support the anatomical classification.

claim: Patients listened to stories spoken by four speakers (two females) with a total duration of 30 min.
source: The patients listened to stories spoken by four speakers (two females) with a total duration of 30 min.
evidence: Directly stated description of the experimental stimulus.

claim: All patients had self-reported normal hearing.
source: All patients had self-reported normal hearing.
evidence: Directly stated patient characteristic.

claim: Eight separate sentences (40 s total) were used as the test data for evaluation of the encoding models.
source: Eight separate sentences (40 s total) were used as the test data for evaluation of the encoding models, and each sentence was repeated six times in a random order.
evidence: Directly stated description of test data.

claim: Each test sentence was repeated six times in a random order.
source: Eight separate sentences (40 s total) were used as the test data for evaluation of the encoding models, and each sentence was repeated six times in a random order.
evidence: Directly stated experimental design detail.

claim: The high-gamma (70–150 Hz) band envelope correlates with neural firing in the proximity of electrodes.
source: We used the envelope of the high-gamma (70–150 Hz) band of the recorded signal as our neural response measure, which correlates with the neural firing in the proximity of electrodes (Ray and Maunsell, 2011; Buzsáki et al., 2012).
evidence: Stated with citations supporting the relationship between high-gamma and neural firing.

claim: Speech-responsive electrodes were selected using a t-test between the average response of each electrode to speech stimuli versus the response in silence (t-value > 2).
source: We restricted our analysis to speech-responsive electrodes, which were selected using a t-test between the average response of each electrode to speech stimuli versus the response in silence (t-value > 2).
evidence: Directly stated selection criterion for electrodes.

claim: The electrode selection criterion resulted in 50 out of 60 electrodes in HG and 47 out of 133 in STG.
source: This criterion resulted in 50 out of 60 electrodes in HG and 47 out of 133 in STG.
evidence: Directly stated result of electrode selection.

claim: Auditory spectrograms were calculated using a model of the peripheral auditory system that estimates a time-frequency representation of the acoustic signal on a tonotopic axis.
source: Auditory spectrograms were calculated using a model of the peripheral auditory system that estimates a time-frequency representation of the acoustic signal on a tonotopic axis (Yang et al., 1992).
evidence: Directly stated method with citation.

claim: The input to the regression models was a sliding window with a duration of 400 ms with 10 ms steps.
source: The input to the regression models was a sliding window with a duration of 400 ms with 10 ms steps, which was found by maximizing the prediction accuracy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to figure showing optimization.

claim: The 400 ms window duration was found by maximizing the prediction accuracy.
source: The input to the regression models was a sliding window with a duration of 400 ms with 10 ms steps, which was found by maximizing the prediction accuracy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Directly stated optimization criterion with supporting figure.

claim: The linear encoding model was a conventional STRF that calculates the linear mapping from stimulus spectrotemporal features to the neural response.
source: The linear encoding model was a conventional STRF that calculates the linear mapping from stimulus spectrotemporal features to the neural response (Theunissen et al., 2001).
evidence: Directly stated model description with citation.

claim: The nonlinear regression model was implemented using a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) consisting of two stages: a feature extraction network and a feature summation network.
source: The nonlinear regression model was implemented using a deep convolutional neural network (CNN; LeCun et al., 1998) consisting of two stages: a feature extraction network and a feature summation network.
evidence: Directly stated model architecture with citation.

claim: The feature extraction network comprises three convolutional layers each with eight 3 × 3 2D convolutional kernels, followed by two convolutional kernels with 1 × 1 kernels to reduce the dimensionality of the representation.
source: The feature extraction network comprises three convolutional layers each with eight 3 × 3 2D convolutional kernels, followed by two convolutional kernels with 1 × 1 kernels to reduce the dimensionality of the representation, thus decreasing the number of model parameters.
evidence: Directly stated architectural details.

claim: The feature summation stage was a two-layer fully connected network with 32 nodes in the hidden layer and a single output node.
source: The feature summation stage was a two-layer fully connected network with 32 nodes in the hidden layer and a single output node.
evidence: Directly stated architectural details.

claim: All hyperparameters of the network were determined by optimizing the prediction accuracy.
source: All hyperparameters of the network were determined by optimizing the prediction accuracy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated optimization procedure with supporting figure.

claim: All hidden layers had rectified linear unit (ReLU) nonlinearity.
source: All hidden layers had rectified linear unit (ReLU) nonlinearity (Nair and Hinton, 2010), and the output node was linear.
evidence: Directly stated architectural detail with citation.

claim: The output node was linear.
source: All hidden layers had rectified linear unit (ReLU) nonlinearity (Nair and Hinton, 2010), and the output node was linear.
evidence: Directly stated architectural detail.

claim: A combination of mean-squared error and Pearson correlation was used as the training loss function.
source: A combination of mean-squared error and Pearson correlation was used as the training loss function (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated training procedure.

claim: The CNN predictions are more similar to the actual responses compared to Lin predictions.
source: As Figure 1B shows, the CNN predictions (red) are more similar to the actual responses (black) compared to Lin predictions (blue).
evidence: Directly stated observation from figure.

claim: The CNN model can capture the variations in the neural responses to speech stimuli more accurately.
source: This observation confirms that the CNN model can capture the variations in the neural responses to speech stimuli more accurately.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the observation of predictions.

claim: CNN predictions show higher accuracy compared to Lin predictions for the majority of electrodes (87 out of 97).
source: Figure 1C shows higher accuracy for CNN predictions compared to Lin predictions for the majority of electrodes (87 out of 97; avg. difference: 0.10; p<<1, t-test).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result with statistical test.

claim: The average difference in prediction accuracy between CNN and Lin is 0.10.
source: Figure 1C shows higher accuracy for CNN predictions compared to Lin predictions for the majority of electrodes (87 out of 97; avg. difference: 0.10; p<<1, t-test).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result.

claim: The overall prediction accuracy is higher for HG electrodes than ones in STG.
source: Even though the overall prediction accuracy is higher for HG electrodes than ones in STG, the absolute improved prediction of CNN over Lin is significantly higher for STG electrodes (avg. improvement 0.07 in HG, 0.13 in STG; p<0.003, two sample one-tailed t-test).
evidence: Directly stated comparison with statistical test.

claim: The absolute improved prediction of CNN over Lin is significantly higher for STG electrodes (avg. improvement 0.07 in HG, 0.13 in STG; p<0.003).
source: Even though the overall prediction accuracy is higher for HG electrodes than ones in STG, the absolute improved prediction of CNN over Lin is significantly higher for STG electrodes (avg. improvement 0.07 in HG, 0.13 in STG; p<0.003, two sample one-tailed t-test).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result with statistical test.

claim: The higher improvement in STG electrodes reveals a larger degree of nonlinearity in the encoding of speech in the STG compared to HG.
source: This higher improvement in STG electrodes reveals a larger degree of nonlinearity in the encoding of speech in the STG compared to HG.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the quantitative results.

claim: All nonlinear models (LN, STP, CNN) improve the prediction accuracy significantly compared to the linear model.
source: Figure 1D shows the improvement of each model over the linear model, averaged separately across electrodes in HG and STG. While all models improve the prediction accuracy significantly compared to the linear model, the CNN accuracy is considerably higher than the other two, particularly in higher auditory areas (STG) which presumably contain more nonlinearities.
evidence: Directly stated with reference to figure showing comparisons.

claim: The CNN accuracy is considerably higher than LN and STP models, particularly in higher auditory areas (STG).
source: Figure 1D shows the improvement of each model over the linear model, averaged separately across electrodes in HG and STG. While all models improve the prediction accuracy significantly compared to the linear model, the CNN accuracy is considerably higher than the other two, particularly in higher auditory areas (STG) which presumably contain more nonlinearities.
evidence: Directly stated comparison with reference to figure.

claim: The CNN predicts the neural responses significantly better than the Lin model even if the duration of the training data is short.
source: Figure 1E also shows that the CNN predicts the neural responses significantly better than the Lin model even if the duration of the training data is short.
evidence: Directly stated observation from figure.

claim: The consistent superiority of the CNN model shows the efficacy of the regularization methods which help avoid the problem of local minima during the training phase.
source: The consistent superiority of the CNN model shows the efficacy of the regularization methods which help avoid the problem of local minima during the training phase.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the model performance.

claim: The dynamic spectrotemporal receptive field (DSTRF) is the linearized equivalent function that the neural network applies to each instance of the stimulus.
source: This equivalent function is found by estimating the derivative of the network output with respect to its input (i.e. the data Jacobian matrix [Wang et al., 2016]). We refer to this linearized equivalent function as the dynamic spectrotemporal receptive field (DSTRF).
evidence: Directly stated definition with citation.

claim: The DSTRF can be considered an STRF whose spectrotemporal tuning depends on every instance of the stimulus.
source: The DSTRF can be considered an STRF whose spectrotemporal tuning depends on every instance of the stimulus.
evidence: Directly stated conceptual description.

claim: Finding the DSTRF is particularly straightforward for a neural network with rectified linear unit nodes (ReLU), because ReLU networks implement piecewise linear functions.
source: Finding the DSTRF is particularly straightforward for a neural network with rectified linear unit nodes (ReLU), because ReLU networks implement piecewise linear functions (Figure 2C).
evidence: Directly stated property with reference to figure.

claim: A rectified linear node is inactive when the sum of its inputs is negative or is active and behaves like a linear function when the sum of its inputs is positive.
source: A rectified linear node is inactive when the sum of its inputs is negative or is active and behaves like a linear function when the sum of its inputs is positive (Figure 2A).
evidence: Directly stated property of ReLU with reference to figure.

claim: The neural network models learn considerably more diverse functions for STG electrodes compared to HG electrodes.
source: The sorted normalized singular values for all electrodes in HG and STG are shown in Figure 2E, demonstrating that the neural network models learn considerably more diverse functions for STG electrodes (statistical analysis provided below).
evidence: Directly stated observation from figure with promise of statistical support.

claim: The complexity of the CNN model is defined as the sum of the normalized singular values of the lag-frequency by time matrix.
source: We defined the complexity of the CNN model as the sum of the normalized singular values of the lag-frequency by time matrix (Figure 2D).
evidence: Directly stated definition with reference to figure.

claim: STG electrodes show significantly higher complexity than HG electrodes (HG avg.: 41.0, STG avg.: 59.7; p<0.001).
source: Figure 2F shows a significantly higher complexity for STG electrodes than for HG electrodes (HG avg.: 41.0, STG avg.: 59.7; p<0.001, two sample t-test), which also correlates with the prediction improvement of each electrode over the linear model (r = 0.66, p<0.001).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result with statistical test.

claim: Complexity correlates with the prediction improvement of each electrode over the linear model (r = 0.66, p<0.001).
source: Figure 2F shows a significantly higher complexity for STG electrodes than for HG electrodes (HG avg.: 41.0, STG avg.: 59.7; p<0.001, two sample t-test), which also correlates with the prediction improvement of each electrode over the linear model (r = 0.66, p<0.001).
evidence: Directly stated correlation with statistical test.

claim: The average number of nodes that switch between active and inactive states at each time step is significantly higher for STG electrodes (p<0.01).
source: The histogram of the average switches for HG and STG electrodes shows significantly higher values for STG electrodes (Figure 2G; p<0.01, one-tailed two sample t-test).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result with statistical test.

claim: The larger improvement of prediction accuracy in STG is due to the implementation of a more diverse set of linear templates.
source: This observation validates the finding that the larger improvement of prediction accuracy in STG is due to the implementation of a more diverse set of linear templates, whereas the HG electrodes require a smaller number of linear functions to accurately capture the stimulus response relationships in this area.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the analysis of node switches.

claim: HG electrodes require a smaller number of linear functions to accurately capture the stimulus response relationships.
source: This observation validates the finding that the larger improvement of prediction accuracy in STG is due to the implementation of a more diverse set of linear templates, whereas the HG electrodes require a smaller number of linear functions to accurately capture the stimulus response relationships in this area.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The hyperparameters and the training of the network can change the internal implementation of the input-output function, but the function itself is robust and remains unchanged.
source: Importantly, these results are not dependent on network parameters and network initialization. While the hyperparameters and the training of the network can change the internal implementation of the input-output function, the function itself is robust and remains unchanged (Materials and methods and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to methods and supplementary figure.

claim: The linearized functions averaged over all samples closely resemble the STRF for the corresponding electrode.
source: Furthermore, the linearized functions averaged over all samples closely resemble the STRF for the corresponding electrode, with the similarity decreasing with the complexity of the neural site (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Directly stated observation with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: The similarity between average DSTRF and STRF decreases with the complexity of the neural site.
source: Furthermore, the linearized functions averaged over all samples closely resemble the STRF for the corresponding electrode, with the similarity decreasing with the complexity of the neural site (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Directly stated relationship with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Three general types of DSTRF variations over time were observed: gain change, temporal hold, and shape change.
source: To investigate the properties of these linearized functions learned by the models for various neural sites, we visually inspected the DSTRFs and observed three general types of variations over time, which we refer to as: I) gain change, II) temporal hold, and III) shape change.
evidence: Directly stated observation from visual inspection.

claim: Gain change refers to the time-varying magnitude of the DSTRF.
source: The first and simplest type of DSTRF change is gain change, which refers to the time-varying magnitude of the DSTRF.
evidence: Directly stated definition.

claim: The variation in the gain of the stimulus-response function learned by the CNN may reflect the nonlinear adaptation of neural responses to the acoustic stimulus.
source: This variation in the gain of the stimulus-response function that is learned by the CNN may reflect the nonlinear adaptation of neural responses to the acoustic stimulus (Abbott, 1997; Rabinowitz et al., 2011; Mesgarani et al., 2014a).
evidence: Stated as an interpretation with citations supporting the concept.

claim: The degree of gain change for each site was quantified by calculating the standard deviation of the DSTRF magnitude over the stimulus duration.
source: We quantified the degree of gain change for each site by calculating the standard deviation of the DSTRF magnitude over the stimulus duration.
evidence: Directly stated quantification method.

claim: Temporal hold refers to the tuning of a site to a fixed spectrotemporal feature but with shifted latency in consecutive time frames.
source: The second type of DSTRF change is temporal hold, which refers to the tuning of a site to a fixed spectrotemporal feature but with shifted latency in consecutive time frames (Figure 3B).
evidence: Directly stated definition with reference to figure.

claim: Temporal hold results in a sustained response to arbitrarily fast spectrotemporal features, hence resembling a short-term memory of that feature.
source: This particular tuning nonlinearity results in a sustained response to arbitrarily fast spectrotemporal features, hence resembling a short-term memory of that feature.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the temporal hold property.

claim: Temporal hold decouples the duration of the response to an acoustic feature from the temporal resolution of that feature.
source: This nonlinear property decouples the duration of the response to an acoustic feature from the temporal resolution of that feature.
evidence: Stated as a functional consequence of temporal hold.

claim: Temporal hold could allow a network to model a slow response to fast acoustic features.
source: For example, temporal hold could allow a network to model a slow response to fast acoustic features.
evidence: Stated as an example of the functional consequence.

claim: A linear increase in the analysis time scale inevitably results in the loss of temporal resolution.
source: This computation cannot be done with a linear operation because a linear increase in the analysis time scale inevitably results in the loss of temporal resolution, as shown in the STRF of site E2 in Figure 3A.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of linear models with reference to figure.

claim: Shape change refers to a change in the spectrotemporal tuning of a site across stimuli.
source: The last dimension of DSTRF variation is shape change, which refers to a change in the spectrotemporal tuning of a site across stimuli.
evidence: Directly stated definition.

claim: A model that implements a more nonlinear function will have a larger number of piecewise linear regions, each exhibiting a different DSTRF shape.
source: Intuitively, a model that implements a more nonlinear function will have a larger number of piecewise linear regions, each exhibiting a different DSTRF shape.
evidence: Stated as an intuitive explanation of shape change.

claim: Shape change is defined as the sum of the normalized singular values of the shift-corrected lag-frequency by time matrix.
source: Therefore, shape change is defined as the sum of the normalized singular values of the shift-corrected lag-frequency by time matrix (Figure 2D).
evidence: Directly stated definition with reference to figure.

claim: The shape change indicates the remaining complexity of the DSTRF function that is not due to temporal hold, or gain change.
source: Thus, the shape change indicates the remaining complexity of the DSTRF function that is not due to temporal hold, or gain change (aligned samples differing only in amplitude are captured by the same set of eigenvectors).
evidence: Stated as an explanation of what shape change captures.

claim: No significant difference was observed between the gain change values in STG and HG sites (HG avg.: 4.6e-3, STG avg.: 4.9e-3; p=0.23).
source: However, we did not observe a significant difference between the gain change values in STG and HG sites (HG avg.: 4.6e-3, STG avg.: 4.9e-3; p=0.23, Wilcoxon rank-sum), suggesting a similar degree of adaptive response in HG and STG sites.
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result with statistical test.

claim: The similar gain change values suggest a similar degree of adaptive response in HG and STG sites.
source: However, we did not observe a significant difference between the gain change values in STG and HG sites (HG avg.: 4.6e-3, STG avg.: 4.9e-3; p=0.23, Wilcoxon rank-sum), suggesting a similar degree of adaptive response in HG and STG sites.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the statistical result.

claim: Temporal hold values are significantly larger in STG sites (HG avg.: 10.1, STG avg.: 15.7; p<1e-4).
source: The distribution of temporal hold values for all sites in the STG and HG shows significantly larger values in STG sites (HG avg.: 10.1, STG avg.: 15.7; p<1e-4, Wilcoxon rank-sum).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result with statistical test.

claim: The increased temporal hold is consistent with previous findings showing increased temporal integration in higher auditory cortical areas.
source: This increased temporal hold is consistent with the previous findings showing increased temporal integration in higher auditory cortical areas (King and Nelken, 2009; Berezutskaya et al., 2017), which allows the stimulus information to be combined across longer time scales.
evidence: Stated as consistency with prior literature with citations.

claim: Increased temporal hold allows the stimulus information to be combined across longer time scales.
source: This increased temporal hold is consistent with the previous findings showing increased temporal integration in higher auditory cortical areas (King and Nelken, 2009; Berezutskaya et al., 2017), which allows the stimulus information to be combined across longer time scales.
evidence: Stated as a functional consequence with citations.

claim: Shape change values are significantly higher on average in STG sites than in HG (HG avg.: 38.8, STG avg.: 46.8; p=0.005).
source: The shape change values are significantly higher on average in STG sites than in HG (HG avg.: 38.8, STG avg.: 46.8; p=0.005, Wilcoxon rank-sum), demonstrating that STG sites have more nonlinear encoding, which requires more diverse receptive field templates than HG sites.
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result with statistical test.

claim: STG sites have more nonlinear encoding, which requires more diverse receptive field templates than HG sites.
source: The shape change values are significantly higher on average in STG sites than in HG (HG avg.: 38.8, STG avg.: 46.8; p=0.005, Wilcoxon rank-sum), demonstrating that STG sites have more nonlinear encoding, which requires more diverse receptive field templates than HG sites.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the shape change results.

claim: The quantified nonlinearity parameters were highly consistent across different network initializations and different segments of the test data.
source: Finally, similar to DSTRF shape, these quantified nonlinearity parameters were highly consistent across different network initializations and different segments of the test data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: The optimal number of clusters for each site was determined using the gap statistic method.
source: The optimal number of clusters for each site was determined using the gap statistic method (Tibshirani et al., 2001).
evidence: Directly stated method with citation.

claim: The optimal number of clusters across all sites differed from 1 to 6.
source: The optimal number of clusters across all sites differed from 1 to 6; the majority of sites, however, contained only one main cluster (84.9% of sites; mean number of clusters = 1.43 ± 1.26 SD).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result.

claim: The majority of sites contained only one main cluster (84.9% of sites; mean number of clusters = 1.43 ± 1.26 SD).
source: The optimal number of clusters across all sites differed from 1 to 6; the majority of sites, however, contained only one main cluster (84.9% of sites; mean number of clusters = 1.43 ± 1.26 SD).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative result.

claim: The three nonlinear parameters (gain change, temporal hold, and shape change) largely predict the complexity of the stimulus-response mapping across sites (r = 0.94, p < 1e-41).
source: The predicted and actual complexity of the models are shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The high correlation value (r = 0.94, p < 1e-41) confirms the efficacy of these three parameters to characterize the complexity of the stimulus-response mapping across sites.
evidence: Directly stated correlation with statistical test.

claim: All three parameters (gain change, temporal hold, shape change) contribute significantly to the overall complexity of DSTRFs in both HG and STG.
source: Moreover, the main effects of the regression (Seber and Lee, 2012) shown in Figure 5A suggest a significant contribution from all three parameters to the overall complexity of DSTRFs in both HG and STG.
evidence: Directly stated result from regression analysis with reference to figure.

claim: The three parameters largely predict stimulus-response nonlinearity (r = 0.76, p < 1e-16).
source: The high correlation values between the actual and predicted improved accuracy (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; r = 0.76, p < 1e-16) show that these three parameters also largely predict stimulus-response nonlinearity.
evidence: Directly stated correlation with statistical test.

claim: The contribution of each nonlinear factor in predicting the improved prediction is different between the HG and STG areas.
source: The contribution of each nonlinear factor in predicting the improved prediction, however, is different between the HG and STG areas, as shown by the main effects of the regression in Figure 5B.
evidence: Directly stated with reference to figure showing regression results.

claim: Gain change (effect = 0.183, p = 0.005) and temporal hold (effect = 0.202, p = 1e-4) factors contributed to the improved accuracy in STG sites.
source: The gain change (effect = 0.183, p = 0.005) and temporal hold (effect = 0.202, p = 1e-4) factors contributed to the improved accuracy in STG sites, while the gain change is the main predictor of the improvement in HG sites (effect = 0.250, p = 2e-5), with a modest contribution from shape change (effect = 0.087, p = 0.028).
evidence: Directly stated regression results with statistical tests.

claim: Gain change is the main predictor of the improvement in HG sites (effect = 0.250, p = 2e-5), with a modest contribution from shape change (effect = 0.087, p = 0.028).
source: The gain change (effect = 0.183, p = 0.005) and temporal hold (effect = 0.202, p = 1e-4) factors contributed to the improved accuracy in STG sites, while the gain change is the main predictor of the improvement in HG sites (effect = 0.250, p = 2e-5), with a modest contribution from shape change (effect = 0.087, p = 0.028).
evidence: Directly stated regression results with statistical tests.

claim: The three types of DSTRF variations are not independent of each other and covary considerably.
source: Notably, the three types of DSTRF variations are not independent of each other and covary considerably (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Sites in STG appear to exhibit multiple nonlinearities simultaneously, making it more difficult to discern their individual contributions.
source: In other words, sites in STG appear to exhibit multiple nonlinearities simultaneously, making it more difficult to discern their individual contributions.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the covariance results.

claim: The improved prediction accuracy using STP model was significant only in STG responses.
source: Interestingly, the prediction accuracy improvement of the STP model was significant only in STG responses.
evidence: Directly stated observation about STP model performance.

claim: The findings are in line with the hypothesis that the gain change nonlinearity captures the nonlinear adaptation of the neural responses to the short-term history of the stimulus.
source: These findings are in line with our hypothesis that the gain change nonlinearity captures the nonlinear adaptation of the neural responses to the short-term history of the stimulus.
evidence: Stated as consistency with hypothesis.

claim: The increasing nonlinearity of the stimulus-response mapping throughout the sensory pathways highlights the critical need for nonlinear computational models of sensory neural processing, particularly in higher cortical areas.
source: The increasing nonlinearity of the stimulus-response mapping throughout the sensory pathways (King and Nelken, 2009; Chechik et al., 2006) highlights the critical need for nonlinear computational models of sensory neural processing, particularly in higher cortical areas.
evidence: Stated with citations supporting the increasing nonlinearity.

claim: Important nonlinear transformations include nonmonotonic and nonlinear stimulus-response functions.
source: These important nonlinear transformations include nonmonotonic and nonlinear stimulus-response functions (Sadagopan and Wang, 2009), time-varying response properties such as stimulus adaptation and gain control (Abbott, 1997; Rabinowitz et al., 2011; Mesgarani et al., 2014a; Dean et al., 2008), and nonlinear interaction of stimulus dimensions and time-varying stimulus encoding (Machens et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: Important nonlinear transformations include time-varying response properties such as stimulus adaptation and gain control.
source: These important nonlinear transformations include nonmonotonic and nonlinear stimulus-response functions (Sadagopan and Wang, 2009), time-varying response properties such as stimulus adaptation and gain control (Abbott, 1997; Rabinowitz et al., 2011; Mesgarani et al., 2014a; Dean et al., 2008), and nonlinear interaction of stimulus dimensions and time-varying stimulus encoding (Machens et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: Important nonlinear transformations include nonlinear interaction of stimulus dimensions and time-varying stimulus encoding.
source: These important nonlinear transformations include nonmonotonic and nonlinear stimulus-response functions (Sadagopan and Wang, 2009), time-varying response properties such as stimulus adaptation and gain control (Abbott, 1997; Rabinowitz et al., 2011; Mesgarani et al., 2014a; Dean et al., 2008), and nonlinear interaction of stimulus dimensions and time-varying stimulus encoding (Machens et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: Nonlinear effects are instrumental in creating robust perception, which requires the formation of invariant perceptual categories from a highly variable stimulus.
source: These nonlinear effects are instrumental in creating robust perception, which requires the formation of invariant perceptual categories from a highly variable stimulus (Leaver and Rauschecker, 2010; Chang et al., 2010; de Heer et al., 2017; Bidelman et al., 2013; Mesgarani et al., 2014b; Steinschneider, 2013; Russ et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Previous extensions of simple receptive field models improve the prediction accuracy of neural responses, but this improvement comes at the cost of reduced interpretability of the computation.
source: Even though all these models improve the prediction accuracy of neural responses, this improvement comes at the cost of reduced interpretability of the computation.
evidence: Stated as a general observation about previous models.

claim: Multifilter extensions of the auditory STRF lead to nonlinear interactions of multiple linear models, which is considerably less interpretable than the STRF model.
source: For example, the multifilter extensions of the auditory STRF (Sharpee et al., 2004; Brenner et al., 2000; Kaardal et al., 2017; Butts et al., 2011; McFarland et al., 2013; Vintch et al., 2015; Harper et al., 2016) lead to nonlinear interactions of multiple linear models, which is considerably less interpretable than the STRF model.
evidence: Stated with citations as an example of reduced interpretability.

claim: The proposed approach extends previous methods by significantly improving the prediction accuracy over the linear, linear-nonlinear, and STP models while remaining highly interpretable.
source: Our approach extends the previous methods by significantly improving the prediction accuracy over the linear, linear-nonlinear, and STP models while at the same time, remaining highly interpretable.
evidence: Stated as a summary of the contribution.

claim: The computational framework can be used in any feedforward neural network model with any number of layers and nodes.
source: The computational framework we propose to explain the neural network function (Nagamine and Mesgarani, 2017) can be used in any feedforward neural network model with any number of layers and nodes, such as in fully connected networks, locally connected networks (Coates and Ay, 2011), or CNNs (LeCun and Bengio, 1995).
evidence: Directly stated generalizability with citations.

claim: One limitation of the DSTRF method is that it cannot be used for neural networks with recurrent connections.
source: Nonetheless, one limitation of the DSTRF method is that it cannot be used for neural networks with recurrent connections.
evidence: Directly stated limitation.

claim: Feedforward models use a fixed duration of the signal as the input, limiting the range of temporal dependencies and contextual effects that can be captured.
source: Because feedforward models use a fixed duration of the signal as the input, the range of the temporal dependencies and contextual effects that can be captured with these models is limited.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of feedforward models.

claim: A small difference was found between the prediction accuracy of feedforward and recurrent neural networks (about 1% improvement in HG, 3% in STG).
source: Although we found only a small difference between the prediction accuracy of feedforward and recurrent neural networks in our data (about 1% improvement in HG, 3% in STG), the recent extensions of the feedforward architecture, such as dilated convolution (Luo and Mesgarani, 2018) or temporal convolutional networks (Lea et al., 2016), can implement receptive fields that extend over long durations.
evidence: Directly stated quantitative comparison.

claim: Recent extensions of the feedforward architecture, such as dilated convolution or temporal convolutional networks, can implement receptive fields that extend over long durations.
source: Although we found only a small difference between the prediction accuracy of feedforward and recurrent neural networks in our data (about 1% improvement in HG, 3% in STG), the recent extensions of the feedforward architecture, such as dilated convolution (Luo and Mesgarani, 2018) or temporal convolutional networks (Lea et al., 2016), can implement receptive fields that extend over long durations.
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: The proposed DSTRF method would seamlessly generalize to dilated convolution and temporal convolutional network architectures.
source: Our proposed DSTRF method would seamlessly generalize to these architectures, which can serve as an alternative to recurrent neural networks when modeling the long-term dependencies of the stimulus is crucial.
evidence: Stated as a potential extension.

claim: The proposed framework combines the ability to capture arbitrary stimulus-response mappings and maintaining model interpretability.
source: In summary, our proposed framework combines two desired properties of a computational sensory-response model; the ability to capture arbitrary stimulus-response mappings and maintaining model interpretability.
evidence: Stated as a summary of the framework's properties.

claim: This data-driven method reveals novel nonlinear properties of cortical representation of speech in the human brain.
source: We showed that this data-driven method reveals novel nonlinear properties of cortical representation of speech in the human brain which provides an example for how it can be used to create more complete neurophysiological models of sensory processing in the brain.
evidence: Stated as a summary of findings.

claim: Deep neural networks are universal function approximators.
source: Moreover, these data-driven models can learn any form of nonlinearity directly from the data without any explicit assumption or prior knowledge of the nonlinearities. This property makes these models particularly suitable for studying the encoding properties of sensory stimuli in the nervous system (Batty et al., 2016; McIntosh et al., 2016; Klindt et al., 2017) whose anatomical and functional organization remains speculative particularly for natural stimuli.
evidence: Stated with citation in the introduction.

claim: A major drawback of DNN models is the difficulty in interpreting the computation that they implement because these models are analytically intractable.
source: A major drawback of DNN models, however, is the difficulty in interpreting the computation that they implement because these models are analytically intractable (the so-called black box property) (Mallat, 2016).
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: The utility of DNNs in leading to novel insights into the computation of sensory nervous systems is lacking.
source: Thus, despite their success in increasing the accuracy of prediction in stimulus-response mapping, their utility in leading to novel insights into the computation of sensory nervous systems is lacking.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of DNNs.

claim: The proposed nonlinear receptive field framework not only more accurately predicts the auditory neural responses, but also uncovers distinct nonlinear encoding properties of speech in primary and nonprimary auditory cortical areas.
source: We demonstrate that not only these models more accurately predict the auditory neural responses, but also uncover distinct nonlinear encoding properties of speech in primary and nonprimary auditory cortical areas.
evidence: Stated as a summary of findings in the introduction.

claim: These findings show the critical need for more complete and interpretable encoding models of neural processing.
source: These findings show the critical need for more complete and interpretable encoding models of neural processing, which can lead to better understanding of cortical sensory processing.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the findings.
